stances.claim: The Supreme Court's progressive liberalization of psychological incapacity -- from Santos and Molina through Tan-Andal -- has produced a nullification regime 'strikingly similar to absolute divorce in foreign jurisdictions.'

Macabata and Amata helpfully reduce the 'case-to-case' uncertainty by formally retaining six Molina guidelines while abandoning the second (expert proof of root cause) and the fourth (medical/clinical incurability) -- replacing the latter with a 'legal sense' of personality incompatibility leading to inevitable and irreparable breakdown.
Abines v. Duque correctly dismissed the Dengvaxia petition on five grounds -- but should have been resolved through a short unsigned resolution since no new doctrine was laid down.

The Court may have violated its constitutional 24-month decision rule: memoranda were required by a Feb. 18, 2020 resolution; the decision was promulgated Sept. 20, 2022 -- beyond the 24-month limit reckoned 'upon the filing of the last pending brief or memorandum.'

one_paragraph_summary: On Valentine's Day eve, Panganiban traces the Supreme Court's progressive liberalization of psychological incapacity (PI) under Article 36 of the Family Code. Imported from Canon Law without prior constitutional, statutory, or jurisprudential precedent, PI was first defined in Santos v. Court of Appeals (Jan. 4, 1995) by gravity, juridical antecedence, and incurability -- and then elaborated in Republic v. Molina (Feb. 13, 1997) into eight guidelines drawn largely from amicus curiae Archbishop Oscar V. Cruz, presiding judge of the Catholic Church's National Appellate Matrimonial Tribunal. The Molina rules proved so strict that very few marriages were nullified, prompting case-by-case relaxations and culminating in Tan-Andal v. Andal (May 11, 2021), which dispensed with the need for expert evidence -- a regime CJ already opined is 'strikingly similar to absolute divorce.' In Macabata v. Macabata (April 6, 2022, reiterated in Republic v. Amata, Nov. 29, 2022), the Court 'refreshingly clarified' that six of the Molina guidelines remain (first, third, fifth, sixth, seventh, and eighth), while the second (expert testimony on 'root cause') and the fourth (medical or clinical permanence/incurability) are set aside -- the latter replaced by a 'legal sense' of personality structures so incompatible and antagonistic as to produce 'inevitable and irreparable breakdown.' He then turns to Abines v. Duque (Sept. 20, 2022, uploaded Feb. 6, 2023), which dismissed a continuing-mandamus petition over Dengvaxia on five grounds: continuing mandamus is limited to ecological rights; ordinary mandamus fails because the acts sought involve discretion; the petition violates the hierarchy of courts; it raises factual questions; and the relief had become moot because the executive branch already acted. While admiring the decision's elegant prose and deep research, Panganiban argues it should have been resolved by a short unsigned resolution since no new doctrine was laid down -- and questions whether the Court complied with the constitutional 24-month rule reckoned from the filing of the last memorandum: the Feb. 18, 2020 memorandum order and the Sept. 20, 2022 promulgation point to a deadline missed. 'Were depth and elegance,' he asks, 'worth the risk of violating the 24-month rule?'
